claim: The plasma membrane in mammalian cells is rich in cholesterol.
source: The plasma membrane in mammalian cells is rich in cholesterol, but how the cholesterol is partitioned between the two leaflets of the plasma membrane remains a matter of debate.
evidence: This is stated as established background information in the abstract, drawing from general scientific knowledge about mammalian cell membranes.

claim: How cholesterol is partitioned between the two leaflets of the plasma membrane remains a matter of debate.
source: The plasma membrane in mammalian cells is rich in cholesterol, but how the cholesterol is partitioned between the two leaflets of the plasma membrane remains a matter of debate.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of scientific discourse and is supported by the existence of conflicting studies in the field.

claim: Liu et al. used domain 4 (D4) of perfringolysin O as a cholesterol sensor.
source: Recently, Liu et al. used domain 4 (D4) of perfringolysin O as a cholesterol sensor to argue that cholesterol is mostly in the exofacial leaflet ( Liu et al., 2017 ).
evidence: This is directly cited from Liu et al., 2017.

claim: Liu et al. argued that cholesterol is mostly in the exofacial leaflet.
source: Recently, Liu et al. used domain 4 (D4) of perfringolysin O as a cholesterol sensor to argue that cholesterol is mostly in the exofacial leaflet ( Liu et al., 2017 ).
evidence: This is the main conclusion from Liu et al., 2017 that is being challenged.

claim: Liu et al. made their conclusion by interpreting D4 binding in live cells using in vitro calibrations with liposomes.
source: This conclusion was made by interpreting D4 binding in live cells using in vitro calibrations with liposomes.
evidence: This describes the methodology used by Liu et al., 2017.

claim: Liposomes may be unfaithful in mimicking the plasma membrane.
source: However, liposomes may be unfaithful in mimicking the plasma membrane, as we demonstrate here.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly Figure 1.

claim: D4 binding is highly sensitive to the presence of cytosolic proteins.
source: Also, D4 binding is highly sensitive to the presence of cytosolic proteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating dose-dependent reduction of D4 binding in the presence of rat liver cytosol.

claim: A D4 variant which requires >35 mol% cholesterol to bind to liposomes in vitro does bind to the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane in a cholesterol-dependent manner.
source: In addition, we find that a D4 variant, which requires >35 mol% cholesterol to bind to liposomes in vitro, does in fact bind to the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane in a cholesterol-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 demonstrating binding of mCherry-D4 variants to the cytoplasmic leaflet and their displacement by cholesterol extraction.

claim: It is unlikely that there is a significantly higher proportion of cholesterol in the exofacial leaflet of the plasma membrane compared to the cytosolic leaflet.
source: Thus, we believe, based on the current evidence, that it is unlikely that there is a significantly higher proportion of cholesterol in the exofacial leaflet of the plasma membrane compared to the cytosolic leaflet.
evidence: This conclusion is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cholesterol constitutes 35–40 mol% of the plasmalemmal lipids according to the majority of studies.
source: The majority of studies have reported that cholesterol constitutes 35–40 mol% of the plasmalemmal lipids (van Meer et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Meer et al., 2008.

claim: Most studies support the notion that there is more cholesterol in the cytoplasmic leaflet than in the exofacial leaflet, or that the balance is close to even.
source: most studies support the notion that there is more cholesterol in the cytoplasmic leaflet than in the exofacial leaflet, or that the balance is close to even (Kobayashi and Menon, 2018; Steck and Lange, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kobayashi and Menon, 2018 and Steck and Lange, 2018.

claim: Liu et al. reported that the abundance of cholesterol in the exofacial leaflet is about an order of magnitude higher than that in the cytoplasmic leaflet.
source: It was surprising, therefore, when Liu et al. reported that the abundance of cholesterol in the exofacial leaflet is about an order of magnitude higher than that in the cytoplasmic leaflet
evidence: This is cited from Liu et al.'s work.

claim: Liu et al. reported that the plasmalemmal cholesterol content is 22–23 mol%.
source: when Liu et al. reported that the abundance of cholesterol in the exofacial leaflet is about an order of magnitude higher than that in the cytoplasmic leaflet, and that the plasmalemmal cholesterol content is 22–23 mol%
evidence: This is cited from Liu et al.'s work.

claim: Liu et al.'s conclusions about cholesterol transbilayer distribution were based on a series of D4 mutants that require different minimum concentrations, or thresholds, of cholesterol in the membrane to bind liposomes in vitro.
source: Their conclusions, particularly the cholesterol transbilayer distribution, were based on a series of D4 mutants that require different minimum concentrations, or thresholds, of cholesterol in the membrane to bind liposomes in vitro.
evidence: This describes the methodology used by Liu et al.

claim: D4 cholesterol binding thresholds may not depend on cholesterol concentrations alone.
source: However, such thresholds may not depend on cholesterol concentrations alone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Phospholipids that surround cholesterol could influence the accessibility of the D4 probes to cholesterol.
source: Phospholipids that surround cholesterol could influence the accessibility of the D4 probes to cholesterol.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1 and by citations to previous literature.

claim: Perfringolysin O (PFO) and its derivatives require a minimum cholesterol concentration, or threshold, in the membrane to bind.
source: For cholesterol-binding, perfringolysin O (PFO) and its derivatives require a minimum cholesterol concentration, or threshold, in the membrane to bind.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PFO and D4 behavior.

claim: The cholesterol binding threshold of PFO is strongly influenced by the membrane phospholipid composition.
source: Such a threshold is known to be strongly influenced by the membrane phospholipid composition (Flanagan et al., 2009; Nelson et al., 2008; Sokolov and Radhakrishnan, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Liu et al. stated that D4 binding is unaffected by phospholipid composition.
source: Although Liu et al. stated that D4 binding is unaffected by phospholipid composition
evidence: This is a statement from Liu et al.'s work.

claim: D4 binding is sensitive to both the acyl chain composition and the phospholipid head group.
source: others have reported that it is sensitive to both the acyl chain composition and the phospholipid head group (He et al., 2017; Maekawa and Fairn, 2015a)
evidence: This is supported by citations to He et al., 2017 and Maekawa and Fairn, 2015a.

claim: DAN-D4 preferentially binds to exofacial leaflet mimic liposomes (PC/SM) over cytoplasmic leaflet mimic liposomes (PC/PE/PS/PI) when both contain 40% cholesterol.
source: As depicted in Figure 1A, for liposomes with constant cholesterol concentration (40%), DAN-D4 preferred the mimic of exofacial leaflet (PC/SM) to the mimic of cytoplasmic leaflet (PC/PE/PS/PI); the amount of D4-DAN that binds the PC/SM liposomes is more than double that which binds PC/PE/PS/PI liposomes.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The threshold for D4 is not identical in liposomes that mimic exofacial and cytoplasmic leaflets of the plasma membrane.
source: Thus, it is evident that the threshold for D4 is not identical in liposomes that mimic exofacial and cytoplasmic leaflets of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 1A.

claim: Varied DAN-D4 binding in vivo cannot be directly interpreted as cholesterol concentration in the plasma membrane.
source: Varied DAN-D4 binding in vivo cannot, therefore, be directly interpreted as cholesterol concentration in the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The phospholipids in the plasma membrane are far more complex than the liposomes used in the study.
source: In addition, the phospholipids in the plasma membrane are far more complex than these liposomes
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of plasma membrane composition.

claim: D4 binding to cholesterol in the membrane depends on the degree of cholesterol exposure in that membrane, as a consequence of cholesterol interactions with surrounding phospholipids.
source: It is known that D4 binding to cholesterol in the membrane depends on the degree of cholesterol exposure in that membrane, as a consequence of cholesterol interactions with surrounding phospholipids (He et al., 2017; Maekawa and Fairn, 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to He et al., 2017 and Maekawa and Fairn, 2015a.

claim: Both head group and acyl chain length impact D4 binding.
source: Both head group and acyl chain length impact D4 binding.
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data.

claim: Acyl chain saturation (the number of double bonds) most significantly influences D4 binding.
source: However, it is the acyl chain saturation, that is, the number of double bonds, that most significantly influences D4 binding (He et al., 2017; Maekawa and Fairn, 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to He et al., 2017 and Maekawa and Fairn, 2015a.

claim: The introduction of a single double bond in phospholipid acyl chains (POPC vs DPPC) significantly enhances DAN-D4 binding to liposomes containing 40 mol% cholesterol.
source: As depicted in Figure 1B, relative to phospholipid with no double bonds in the acyl chain (DPPC, 16:0,16:0), the introduction of a single double bond (POPC, 16:0, 18:1) significantly enhanced the binding of the DAN-D4 to the liposomes.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DAN-D4 binding is further elevated when two double bonds are introduced in phospholipid acyl chains (DOPC).
source: The DAN-D4 binding was further elevated when two double bonds were introduced (DOPC, 18:1, 18:1).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Liu et al. did not systematically test the effect of acyl chain saturation in phospholipids most abundant in the plasma membrane.
source: Although Liu et al. did study the effects of phospholipid composition on D4 binding (supplementary 1h and i), they did not systematically test the effect of acyl chain saturation in phospholipids, particularly those most abundant in the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an observation about the methodology in Liu et al.'s work.

claim: Both acyl chain saturation and phospholipid head group significantly impact DAN-D4 binding to liposomes.
source: Nevertheless, our experiments clearly demonstrate that both acyl chain saturation and phospholipid head group significantly impact DAN-D4 binding to liposomes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Liu et al. could have underestimated the cholesterol content in the cytoplasmic leaflet of plasma membrane.
source: The fact that DAN-D4 binding to the cytoplasmic leaflet-like liposomes was significantly attenuated, compared to those that mimic the exofacial leaflet, suggests that Liu et al. could have underestimated the cholesterol content in the cytoplasmic leaflet of plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing differential binding to different liposome compositions.

claim: The lipid classes and species in live cells are significantly more complex than the liposomes used in the study.
source: More importantly, as the lipid classes and species in live cells are significantly more complex than the liposomes we used here
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of cellular lipid composition.

claim: Liposome-based calibration cannot be regarded as a true proxy for D4 binding to the exofacial and cytoplasmic leaflets of the plasma membrane.
source: it is unlikely that the liposome-based calibration, as in the approach employed by Liu et al., could be regarded as a true proxy for D4 binding to the exofacial and cytoplasmic leaflets of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and complexity of cellular membranes.

claim: Quantitative interpretation of D4 binding in live cells is extremely difficult, if at all possible, even with multiple rigorous calibrations.
source: Quantitative interpretation of D4 binding in live cells is extremely difficult, if at all possible, even with multiple rigorous calibrations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings and the complexity of the cellular environment.

claim: The cytoplasm is very rich in proteins, which could further complicate the binding of D4 to cholesterol.
source: Additionally, within cells, the cytoplasm is very rich in proteins, which could further complicate the binding of D4 to cholesterol (see below).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of cytoplasmic composition and is supported by experimental data in Figure 1C.

claim: Liu et al. reported that microinjected D4 and the variants D4D434A and D4D434A, A463W failed to bind to the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: Liu et al. reported that microinjected D4 and the variants D4D434A and D4D434A, A463W, failed to bind to the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Liu et al., 2017.

claim: The lack of binding of microinjected D4 variants to the cytoplasmic leaflet was Liu et al.'s key evidence to conclude that there is little cholesterol in the cytoplasmic leaflet.
source: This was their key evidence to conclude that there is little cholesterol in the cytoplasmic leaflet.
evidence: This describes the reasoning in Liu et al.'s work.

claim: Both wild-type D4 and a D434S mutant are capable of binding to the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: This observation was surprising as it has been reported previously that both wild-type D4 and a D434S mutant (comparable to D434A) are capable of binding to the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane (Maekawa and Fairn, 2015b; Abe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maekawa and Fairn, 2015b and Abe et al., 2012.

claim: The microinjected DAN-D4 proteins may not have been behaving as expected.
source: This raises the possibility that the microinjected DAN-D4 proteins were not behaving as expected.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between Liu et al.'s results and previous reports.

claim: The presence of cytosolic proteins is a potential confounder that would interfere with DAN-D4 binding to cholesterol in the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: One of the potential confounders is the presence of cytosolic proteins, which would interfere with DAN-D4 binding to cholesterol in the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is speculation supported by experimental data in Figure 1C.

claim: DAN-D4 could bind cytosolic proteins, which would titrate away the microinjected DAN-D4 and prevent DAN-D4 from binding to the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: DAN-D4 could bind cytosolic proteins, which would titrate away the microinjected DAN-D4 and prevent DAN-D4 from binding to the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is speculation supported by experimental data in Figure 1C.

claim: The protein concentration in cells is estimated to be about 100 mg/ml.
source: The protein concentration in cells is estimated to be about 100 mg/ml (Zeskind et al., 2007; Luby-Phelps, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zeskind et al., 2007 and Luby-Phelps, 2000.

claim: Even weak affinity of DAN-D4 to cytosolic proteins could reduce the effective concentration available for binding to membranes at high protein concentrations.
source: With such a high protein concentration, even weak affinity of DAN-D4 to cytosolic proteins could reduce the effective concentration available for binding to membranes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high protein concentration in cells and experimental data.

claim: The inclusion of rat liver cytosol in the binding assay reduced DAN-D4 binding to liposomes in a dose-dependent manner.
source: As depicted in Figure 1C, the inclusion of RLC in the binding assay reduced DAN-D4 binding to the liposomes in a dose-dependent manner
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Rat liver cytosol at 1.5 mg/ml causes almost complete ablation of DAN-D4 binding to liposomes.
source: the inclusion of RLC in the binding assay reduced DAN-D4 binding to the liposomes in a dose-dependent manner with an almost complete ablation of binding at 1.5 mg/ml.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The capability of microinjected DAN-D4 to bind the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane could be severely diminished in live cells, regardless of cholesterol content in the membrane.
source: Thus, the capability of microinjected DAN-D4 to bind the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane could be severely diminished in live cells, regardless of cholesterol content in the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing protein interference with D4 binding.

claim: mCherry-D4 and mCherry D4D434S have been shown previously to bind to the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: mCherry-D4 and mCherry D4D434S have been shown previously to bind to the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is based on previous published work.

claim: Exogenously expressed mCherry-D4D434A and mCherry-D4D434A,A463W bind to the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, exogenously expressed mCherry-D4D434A and mCherry-D4D434A,A463W, in fact, do bind to the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: mCherry-tagged D4 probes are responsive to changes in cholesterol and are displaced from the cytoplasmic leaflet following extraction of plasmalemmal cholesterol by methyl-β-cyclodextrin.
source: Importantly, these mCherry-tagged probes were responsive to changes in cholesterol: they were displaced from the cytoplasmic leaflet following extraction of the plasmalemmal cholesterol by methyl-β-cyclodextrin (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The lack of binding of the DAN-D4 variants shown by Liu et al. is not likely to result from insufficient cholesterol in the cytoplasmic leaflet.
source: Thus, the lack of binding of the DAN-D4 variants, as shown by Liu and colleagues, is not likely to result from insufficient cholesterol in the cytoplasmic leaflet.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that mCherry-D4 variants do bind to the cytoplasmic leaflet.

claim: Liberation of mCherry-D4 variants from the plasma membrane following cholesterol extraction is accompanied by the appearance of bright puncta within the cytosol.
source: Noticeably, liberation of the mCherry-D4 variants from the PM following cholesterol extraction is accompanied by the appearance of bright puncta within the cytosol.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data in Figure 2B.

claim: The appearance of bright puncta in the cytosol after cholesterol extraction cannot be a result of a sudden increase in endomembrane cholesterol.
source: This cannot be a result of a sudden increase in endomembrane cholesterol, as acute cholesterol extraction would only lower cellular cholesterol, including endomembranes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the logic that cholesterol extraction reduces total cellular cholesterol.

claim: Without cholesterol-rich membrane to bind, D4 could form aggregates within the cytoplasm or be bound to unidentified membrane structures.
source: However, without cholesterol-rich membrane to bind, D4 could form aggregates within the cytoplasm or be bound to unidentified membrane structures.
evidence: This is speculation about the nature of the bright puncta observed after cholesterol extraction.

claim: A 10-fold enrichment of cholesterol in the exofacial leaflet over the cytoplasmic leaflet would be significant in membrane biology and physiology.
source: It would be significant in membrane biology and physiology if there was a 10-fold enrichment of cholesterol in the exofacial leaflet over that in the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of membrane biology.

claim: Generation and maintenance of a 10-fold cholesterol gradient would be an ATP-consuming process, incurring a huge energy demand.
source: In particular, Liu et al. (2017), concluded that generation and maintenance of such a 10-fold gradient would be an ATP-consuming process, incurring a huge energy demand
evidence: This is cited from Liu et al., 2017.

claim: Cholesterol can flip spontaneously in membranes with a t1/2<1 s.
source: as cholesterol can flip spontaneously in membranes with a t1/2<1 s (Steck and Lange, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Steck and Lange, 2018.

claim: The data reported in the study by Liu et al. cannot be extrapolated to provide precise measurements of cholesterol, especially for the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: Here we have repeated and extended vital control experiments and found that the data reported in the study by Liu et al. cannot be extrapolated to provide precise measurements of cholesterol, especially for the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Full-length PFO toxin and recombinant D4 have been studied extensively for their ability to bind cholesterol.
source: Full-length PFO toxin and recombinant D4 have been studied extensively for their ability to bind cholesterol.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Neighboring phospholipids influence the ability of D4 to sense and bind to cholesterol.
source: It is known that neighboring phospholipids influence the ability of D4 to sense and bind to cholesterol.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and is supported by experimental data.

claim: Cholesterol has to be shielded from the aqueous environment by surrounding phospholipids because of its small hydroxyl head group.
source: Because of its small hydroxyl head group, cholesterol has to be shielded from the aqueous environment by surrounding phospholipids.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of cholesterol structure and membrane organization.

claim: The degree of cholesterol shielding is influenced by the lateral packing of lipids (both the acyl chain composition of the lipids and the structure of the head group).
source: The degree of shielding is influenced by the lateral packing of lipids (i.e., both the acyl chain composition of the lipids as well as the structure of the head group).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of membrane biophysics.

claim: When included with lipids with unsaturated acyl chains such as DOPC, cholesterol is more readily accessible by D4 than when in membranes with saturated DPPC.
source: Thus, when included with lipids with unsaturated acyl chains, such as DOPC, cholesterol is more readily accessible by D4 than when in membranes with saturated DPPC (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: D4 recognizes accessible or chemically active cholesterol, not bulk or total cholesterol.
source: This observation alone demonstrates that D4 recognizes accessible or chemically active cholesterol, not bulk or total cholesterol.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing differential binding to membranes with the same cholesterol content but different phospholipid compositions.

claim: The addition of the lipophilic DAN or Nile red derivative may increase the affinity of D4 variants to cytosolic proteins.
source: One possibility is that the addition of the lipophilic DAN or the Nile red derivative, as used by Liu and colleagues, may increase the affinity of D4 variants to cytosolic proteins.
evidence: This is speculation supported by experimental data in Figure 1C.

claim: mCherry is not likely to alter the affinity of D4 to cytosolic proteins.
source: mCherry is not likely to alter the affinity of D4 to cytosolic proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of mCherry and the experimental results.

claim: D4 sensors will have to compete with endogenous cholesterol-binding proteins for the accessible pool of cholesterol in membranes.
source: Regardless of the fluorophore attached to the D4, the sensors will have to compete with endogenous cholesterol-binding proteins for the accessible pool of cholesterol in membranes.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of cellular cholesterol-binding proteins.

claim: Genetically coded biosensors for phospholipids have been used by cell biologists for two decades.
source: Genetically coded biosensors for phospholipids have been used by cell biologists for two decades.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of the field.

claim: Lipid and cholesterol sensors such as D4 must be interpreted with rigor.
source: However, lipid and cholesterol sensors such as D4 must be interpreted with rigor.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the manuscript.

claim: Cholesterol partitioning between leaflets in the plasma membrane is complicated to assess by D4 binding because cholesterol can spontaneously flip-flop between leaflets of a bilayer.
source: In particular, cholesterol partitioning between leaflets in the plasma membrane is even more complicated to assess by such binding, as cholesterol can spontaneously flip-flop between leaflets of a bilayer (Leventis and Silvius, 2001).
evidence: This is based on citation to Leventis and Silvius, 2001.

claim: The binding of cholesterol by an exogenous membrane-impermeant probe on the exofacial surface would likely trap cholesterol and alter the cholesterol distribution.
source: Thus, the binding of cholesterol by an exogenous membrane-impermeant probe on the exofacial surface would likely trap cholesterol and alter the cholesterol distribution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid flip-flop of cholesterol and the binding properties of D4.

claim: Binding ~1% of the cholesterol in the exofacial leaflet using a D4 homolog was sufficient to trigger a 'lack of cholesterol' signal on the ER membrane inside cells.
source: This situation was elegantly illustrated in a recent paper, where binding ~1% of the cholesterol in the exofacial leaflet using a D4 homolog was sufficient to trigger a 'lack of cholesterol' signal on the ER membrane inside the cells (Infante and Radhakrishnan, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Infante and Radhakrishnan, 2017.

claim: D4 and its derivatives are useful in some focused studies to make endpoint measurements or inhibit cholesterol trafficking.
source: Although D4 and its derivatives are useful in some focused studies to make endpoint measurements or inhibit cholesterol trafficking
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the properties of D4 and previous literature.

claim: D4 tools cannot be used to assess cholesterol partitioning between two leaflets of plasma membranes in live cells.
source: we conclude that these tools cannot be used to assess cholesterol partitioning between two leaflets of plasma membranes in live cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript based on all the experimental data and reasoning presented.
